criteria.justification: The response explicitly reframes the issue as 'no longer a naming problem; it is a stakeholder management and UX problem' and diagnoses the pattern (asking a short name to do too much work, chasing a 'perfect' zero-confusion name) rather than just re-picking a candidate name for round four.

The response proposes convening veto-holders up front, setting the rule to choose 'the least worst name, not a perfect name,' and locking the decision so 'No one is allowed to reopen the naming decision in a later cycle unless a catastrophic legal/compliance issue arises,' explicitly invoking 'Disagree and Commit.'

The response treats each prior objection as legitimate and designs around it (lexicon constraint for Round 2, UX copy for Round 1), and implicitly acknowledges diminishing returns by noting 'no 3-word name can explain a complex risk variance,' but it never explicitly weighs whether the repeated reopening reflects genuinely new information versus re-litigation of the same settled tradeoffs.

The response directly incorporates the locked API name, proposing to 'make the customer-facing name a direct, plain-English translation of the API field name' to avoid dev/support friction, rather than ignoring or reopening that architecture.

The response explicitly contrasts its approach with prior rounds by shifting explanatory burden from the name itself to mandatory UX copy ('A name cannot explain a methodology. That is what UI copy is for') and by pre-securing buy-in from the specific reviewers who killed prior rounds, rather than proposing another ad hoc name in isolation.
